The Final, Part Two
The last over of the World Cup. You're on ninety-six. Twelve to win. Harpreet is at the other end. Harpreet cannot be allowed to face a ball.

On the big screen, between overs, they show the Indian dugout. In the corner, leaning on a crutch, in a grey hoodie and track pants, is Aryan Khurana. He flew in this morning. He's shouting something at the screen.
KUTTANAD! ONE MORE! ONE MORE!
He's holding up a hand-drawn sign. It's a snake boat. Badly drawn. Next to it, in big letters: "ROW."
Kuttanad. Two thousand people. Nobody is breathing. Shibu's mother is holding a candle. Father Joseph is holding two.
Corrigan runs in. Sixty thousand people roar. Your hands are perfectly steady for the first time in your life.
12 off 6
The World Cup final. Last wicket. The fastest bowler in the world. Your mother is in the stands. Twelve to win.
WORLD CHAMPIONS!
Dropped nine times. Never again.
SO CLOSE
Sixty thousand people stand for you anyway.
The last ball is short and fast and it goes higher than anything you've ever hit. It lands in the top tier.
Your hundred. The World Cup. In the same second.
You don't celebrate. You touch your collar. Then you drop your bat, kneel on the pitch, and mime rowing. Your whole team runs onto the field and kneels behind you, and rows with you.
WORLD CHAMPIONS! You hear me, Kuttanad? WORLD CHAMPIONS!
Last ball. Two to win. You hit it hard and true to deep cover, and you run like your life depends on it, and the throw beats Harpreet by a foot.
Ninety-nine not out. Runners-up by one run. You sit down on the pitch, and the first person to reach you isn't a teammate.
It's Corrigan. He pulls you up and holds your hand in the air.
One run. ONE run. Look at me. You took us from forty for four to one run. Nobody will ever forget this innings. Nobody.
Later. The dressing room is chaos. Somebody's playing film songs from a phone in a bucket. The door opens and Amma walks in, in her big coat, and the whole team goes quiet and stands up.
Sit, sit. I only came to tell my son he looks thin.
And to tell all of you: you rowed with him. Thank you.
Press conference in ten minutes.
I've asked to go first.
I only have one question. It isn't about cricket.
Two hundred journalists. A wall of cameras. Diya stands up at the front, holding a notebook she isn't reading.
Diya Nair. Kerala. My question is simple. What happens now?
"Now I go home and row in a boat race."
The truth, and a promise.
"Now I take a reporter for some terrible coffee."
In front of two hundred journalists.
Diya Nair. Kerala. You told me to ask you after the final. It's after the final.
"Yes. The answer is yes."
"Ask me again in Kuttanad. At the boat race."
Somewhere that's yours.
The room explodes. Two hundred journalists, and every single one of them is writing the same line.
It's over. Now there's only one place left to go.
